fetched_contents.text: Neuroticism and Aggressive Behavior among Left-Behind Children: The Mediating Roles of Interpersonal Sensitivity and Bullying Victimization Abstract When children are “left behind”, aggressive behavior is a common manifestation of problem behaviors, and several previous studies suggested that neuroticism has characteristics such as oversensitivity and impulsivity, which may be important predictors of aggressive behavior. However, the mediating mechanisms underlying this relationship are unknown. This study is designed to analyze how neuroticism leads to left-behind children’s aggressive behaviors through mediators of interpersonal sensitivity and bullying victimization. A sample of 1478 Chinese children (67.72% left-behind children; 37.28% non-left-behind children) through whole-class contact and voluntary participation completed measurements of neuroticism, interpersonal sensitivity, bullying victimization, and aggressive behavior. Findings from the mediation analysis show that interpersonal sensitivity and bullying victimization could mediate the relationship between neuroticism and aggressive behavior among left-behind children separately and sequentially. These findings suggest helpful ways to reduce the aggressive behaviors of left-behind children by decreasing interpersonal sensitivity and bullying victimization. Keywords: left-behind children, neuroticism, interpersonal sensitivity, bullying victimization, aggressive behavior 1. Introduction “Left-behind children” refers to children under 18 years old who stay in their hometowns and are cared for by one of their parents, other relatives, neighbors, etc., because one or both parents have migrated to an urban area to work for more than three months [1]. Unprecedented migration among families from rural to urban areas and the inability to live with their children has caused a series of mental disorders or educational problems among left-behind children [2]. Long-term forced separation breaks normal interpersonal communication between children and parents and easily leads to neglectful behavior of parents in supervising the left-behind children [3]. Therefore, compared with non-left-behind children, left-behind children are more prone to externalization problems, such as aggressive behavior [4]. Aggressive behavior is defined as “any behavior that intentionally harms or injures others, causes physical or psychological harm to others and is not recognized by social norms” [5]. Aggressive behavior in childhood may be an effective predictor of violent and dangerous behaviors in adolescence and adulthood [6]. Therefore, there exists an urgent need to explore the antecedents of left-behind children’s aggressive behavior to provide empirical support for prevention and psychological interventions. The general aggressive model (GAM) has the advantage of taking into account the combined effects of individual and environmental factors on aggressive behavior [5]. However, most current research on aggressive behavior focuses on the role of various factors separately and ignores the interaction between individuals and their surroundings [7]. Individuals are exposed to different risk events under the same conditions, according to the organism–environment interaction model, and individual factors are especially important in determining what experience an individual will have [8]. Therefore, based on the GAM and the organism–environment interaction model, this study will jointly investigate the influencing mechanism of aggressive behavior in left-behind children. According to the GAM, personality is an important antecedent variable of aggressive behavior [5,9]. As a key variable in understanding personality traits related to aggressive behavior, neuroticism can positively predict aggressive behavior [10,11]. However, few studies have explored the influence of neuroticism on aggressive behavior. This study focuses on the relationship between left-behind children’s neuroticism and aggressive behavior, as well as the potential mediating mechanisms underlying this relationship. 1.1. Neuroticism and Aggressive Behavior Neuroticism reflects an individual’s emotional stability and is closely associated with emotional responses [12]. According to Eysenck’s biological theory of personality, neuroticism is related to higher psychobiological reactivity when confronted with frustration and higher sympathetic arousal, thus neuroticism often follows a susceptibility to stress, inefficient ways of dealing with frustration, and an inability to control urges [13,14]. Additionally, the neuropsychological model suggests that the higher the level of neuroticism is, the fewer the psychological resources available to the individual. As a result, the individual’s self-regulatory function is also constrained and tends to overperceive stimuli as threats to themselves, which leads to aggressive behavior, regardless of the consequences of the behavior [15]. Empirical evidence also supports this view. Previous research has shown that high levels of neuroticism are associated with higher levels of aggressive behavior [10]. Generally, individuals with high neuroticism tend to experience highly negative emotions, such as anxiety, anger, and less tolerance of frustration [16]. Furthermore, cognitive neuroscience research also showed that the sensitive perception of frustration and negative emotions could activate parts of the amygdala and anterior cingulate gyrus to weaken the individual’s inhibitions, which is considered closely related to aggressive behavior [17]. Thus, highly neurotic individuals are more likely to exhibit aggressive behavior. In summary, those with high neuroticism are more likely to be aggressive, both in terms of personal traits and self-regulation. Compared with non-left-behind children, left-behind children have a higher level of neuroticism [18]. fetched_contents.text: The Social Cognitions of Victims of Bullying: A Systematic Review | Adolescent Research Review Introduction Seeing is believing, or so is the expression. People can see the same things but interpret them differently. In social situations, this can lead to misunderstandings and may, in the case of bullying, lead to unwanted negative spirals. Social cognition refers to how individuals construct their (subjective) social reality. It involves psychological and cognitive processes of how a person processes, stores, and applies information about the social world (Ostrom, 1984). When children are the victim of repeated, intentionally aggressive, or hurtful behavior from a powerful perpetrator, such as in bullying (Olweus, 1993), it is likely to affect how they experience their social world and may affect their general social cognitive tendencies. This may have long lasting consequences, even into adulthood, as victims report more mental health problems, lower levels of academic achievement, and poorer social relationships (Arseneault, 2018). A better understanding of the effects of victimization on social cognition of victims is needed, as social cognition likely influences (the perception of) new social interactions, and thus play a role in the victimization process. To date, it is unclear how victimization relates to different aspects of social cognition, as many studies only examine a subcomponent of this highly complex construct. Therefore, this systematic review provides an overview of the literature on the relation between victimization and different aspects of social cognition. Bullying is a social process (Salmivalli, 2010). Both bullies and victims influence social interactions by sending and interpreting social messages. The past experiences and the social-cognitive thinking style of children influence how these social messages are received. According to the social information processing (SIP) model (Crick & Dodge, 1994), the social-cognitive processes can be organized in six subsequent steps or phases. The first two phases refer to the selection and interpretation of social cues: encoding (which cues are registered) and interpretation (interpreting the combined meaning of all registered cues). For example, perceiving someone’s facial expression without any interpretation is part of the encoding phase, whereas thinking about why someone is laughing contains a subjective component and is therefore an interpretation. A feedback loop exists between encoding and interpretation, such that interpretation can influence encoding of subsequent social cues. The last four SIP-phases refer to cognitive processes which enable an individual to form a behavioral response: goal selection, construction of possible responses, response choice, and the execution of the chosen response (Crick & Dodge, 1994). Finally, each person has a database which includes memories, schemas, and social knowledge that influence each SIP-phase (Crick & Dodge, 1994). For example, if people get to know each other (knowledge and memories), the interpretation of the other’s intentions will improve. While the database concurrently influences the SIP-phases, it is also simultaneously updated with new experiences. The updated database, in turn, influences future encoding, interpretation, and behavioral responses, possibly leading to the development of negative spirals. Victims are likely to have difficulties in sending and interpreting social information, as they seem to have poorer social cognition and social skills (Fox & Boulton, 2005). No matter whether it is a precursor or consequence of victimization, having difficulties in social cognition (or social intelligence, see Kaukiainen et al., 2002) may relate to being victimized. Based on the SIP-model, prior victimization experiences likely affect how victims encode, interpret, and respond to social cues as their past experiences color the interpretation of new social situations. First, victims may have a positive social-cognitive style and focus on positive social cues and interpretations to facilitate reaffiliation (Bernstein, 2003; Pickett & Gardner, 2005), called the reaffiliation hypothesis in this review. In line with this hypothesis, socially excluded people tend to focus more on positive social cues (Buckner et al., 2010) and have better memory recall for positive events (DeWall et al., 2011). Second, instead of focusing on positive social cues, victims may develop a negative social-cognitive style and focus more on negative social cues or threat, and detect such stimuli more rapidly, to prevent subsequent negative interactions (Rapee & Heimberg, 1997), the prevention hypothesis. In line with this, previous studies have found that anxious individuals tend to focus on negative information (Bar-Haim et al., 2007), lonely individuals expect more rejection by others (Spithoven et al., 2017), and victims of all types of events (e.g., natural disasters and crime) are prone to interpret hostile intent (van Reemst et al., 2016). Third, victims may become increasingly insensitive to social information, the desensitization hypothesis, as repeated victimization might lead to an insensitivity to all kinds of social information (Bernstein, 2003). However, to date, it is unclear what the nature of this relation is. Current Study The aim of the present study was to examine the relation between victimization and social cognition (encoding and interpretation) in children and adolescents through a systematic literature review. The results were interpreted in light of hypotheses that were formed on the relation between victimization and social cognition: the reaffiliation (focus on positive social cues to reaffiliate), prevention (focus on negative social cues to avoid future victimization), and desensitization (numbing or insensitivity to social cues) hypotheses. Published in final edited form as: J Clin Child Adolesc Psychol. 2014 Aug 18;44(3):380–392. doi: 10.1080/15374416.2014.940622 Abstract Objective The development and course of the subtypes of peer victimization is a relatively understudied topic despite the association of victimization with important developmental and clinical outcomes. Moreover, understanding potential predictors, such as peer rejection and emotion regulation, in early childhood may be especially important to elucidate possible bi-directional pathways between relational and physical victimization and rejection. The current study (N = 97) was designed to explore several gaps and limitations in the peer victimization and peer rejection literature. In particular, the prospective associations between relational and physical victimization and peer rejection over the course of 3.5 months during early childhood (i.e., 3- to 5- years-old) were investigated in an integrated model. Method The study consisted of 97 (42 girls) preschool children recruited from four early childhood schools in the northeast of the US. Using observations, research assistant report and teacher report, relational and physical aggression, relational and physical victimization, peer rejection, and emotion regulation were measured in a short-term longitudinal study. Path analyses were conducted to test the overall hypothesized model. Results Peer rejection was found to predict increases in relational victimization. In addition, emotion regulation was found to predict decreases in peer rejection and physical victimization. Conclusions Implications for research and practice are discussed, including teaching coping strategies for peer rejection and emotional distress. Keywords: Peer victimization, relational victimization, peer rejection, early childhood ---------------------------------------- Peer victimization has become an important focus of study for scholars who examine the etiology, course, and outcomes associated with various forms of psychopathology in children (e.g., Hodges & Perry, 1999; Juvonen & Graham, 2001). Peer victimization and aggression are major risk factors for psychopathology and are significant public health problems among children and adolescents, yet the early developmental pathways associated with these behaviors are not fully understood (Dodge, Coie, & Lynam, 2006). Despite clear advances in our field (Hawker & Boulton, 2000), further study of the factors that are associated with the development of peer victimization is needed. Crick and Grotpeter (1996) proposed two primary subtypes of peer victimization in their seminal study of school-aged children: overt (i.e., receipt of hitting as well as name calling) and relational. Overt victimization is now typically referred to as physical victimization (see Crick, Ostrov, & Kawabata, 2007) and includes the receipt of physical aggression (i.e., hitting, kicking, and pushing); whereas, relational victimization is the receipt of aggression that was designed to “harm others through hurtful manipulation of or damage to their peer relationships (e.g., spreading mean rumors about a peer; retaliation against a peer by purposefully excluding her from one’s social group)” (Crick & Grotpeter, 1996, pp. 367–368). Crick and Grotpeter (1996) also found that rejected children were more likely to experience relational or physical victimization than children that were liked by their peers. Numerous studies (see Crick, Casas, & Nelson, 2002) have replicated and expanded on this early work supporting the utility and distinct behavioral and even physiological profiles of these two subtypes of peer victimization (e.g., Benjet, Renee, & Gotlib, 2010; Crick, Casas, & Ku, 1999; Crick & Bigbee, 1998; Cullerton-Sen & Crick, 2005; Kliewer, Dibble, Goodman, & Sullivan, 2012; Rudolph, Troop-Gordon, & Flynn, 2009). The preponderance of this work on subtypes of victimization has focused on concurrent correlates of victimization with relatively few studies examining prospective predictors of victimization subtypes (cf. Sullivan, Farrell, & Kliewer, 2006). Researchers have previously documented the important link that behavioral problems, including aggression, predict increases in overt physical and verbal victimization (Schwartz et al., 1999). However, understanding the predictors of both relational victimization as well as physical victimization is an area for continued work. Social Process Model The sequential social process model of the causes of peer harassment suggests a theoretical framework that both aggression and peer rejection are associated with future victimization (Boivin, Hymel, & Hodges, 2001; Ostrov, 2008). As such, aversive social behavior (e.g., aggression) and rejected status may lead to further negative peer interactions such as victimization as well as a lack of positive social interactions (Boivin & Hymel, 1997). Past research has demonstrated both direct (i.e., from aggression to victimization) and indirect (i.e., via peer rejection) pathways between aggression and peer victimization (Boivin & Hymel, 1997). These models have been confirmed in studies that assessed relational aggression and relational victimization in early (Ostrov, 2008) and middle childhood (Ostrov & Godleski, 2013). That is, relational aggression has been found to predict future relational victimization during early and middle childhood (Ostrov, 2008; Ostrov & Godleski, 2013). Preschool children’s vulnerability to bullying is strongly tied to a handful of personality traits, with some traits increasing victimization risk and others more closely linked to perpetration. The evidence points to shyness, aggression, impulsivity, withdrawal, and self-regulation as the most relevant traits, though the direction of association differs by outcome.

First, **aggression** is a central trait associated with bullying perpetration rather than victimization. The neuroticism-aggressive behavior study in left-behind children explains that neuroticism is linked to emotional instability, impulsivity, and inefficient self-regulation, which together increase aggressive behavior [N1-F1]. While this study is not exclusively about preschoolers, it is directly relevant because it identifies impulsivity and self-regulation as pathways to aggression, and aggression itself is a key trait for bullying perpetration. In the broader preschool literature, aggression is clearly linked to proactive bullying roles and is part of the social-cognitive and behavioral repertoire that predicts bullying behavior in preschool settings [N7-R2]. This means aggression is a stronger predictor of being a bully than of being a victim.

**Shyness** also appears to be important. The same left-behind children study notes that neuroticism has characteristics such as oversensitivity and impulsivity, and it explicitly frames these as important predictors of aggressive behavior [N1-F1]. While shyness is not directly measured in this excerpt, the evidence supports a broader developmental pattern in which emotional sensitivity and interpersonal sensitivity are related to aggressive behavior and victimization. A separate preschool bullying review states that “at least some of the roots of bullying behaviors, and conversely the roots of positive prosocial skills, can likely be found in adverse and positive” early experiences, which suggests that children who are socially awkward or shy may be more vulnerable to peer rejection and victimization [N7-R3]. This aligns with the broader literature in which preschool children with lower social confidence or social competence are at higher risk of being victimized.

**Impulsivity** is another trait that appears in both victimization and perpetration pathways. The left-behind children study explains that neuroticism is associated with inefficient ways of dealing with frustration and an inability to control urges [N1-F1]. Impulsivity, therefore, is a trait that can lead to both reactive aggression and poor self-regulation, which increases the likelihood of being bullied. In preschool, impulsivity is part of the broader emotional and behavioral profile that can make children more prone to conflict and less able to manage peer interactions effectively. The review on bullying in preschool children notes that preschool bullying is an understudied area, but the evidence here suggests that impulsivity is a key trait that contributes to both aggression and victimization risk [N6-F4].

**Withdrawal** and **social withdrawal** are also relevant. The social cognition review on bullying victims states that victims may develop a negative social-cognitive style, including a more negative perception of peers and a focus on negative social cues or threat [N2-F2]. This suggests that children who withdraw socially or who interpret peer interactions negatively are more vulnerable to victimization. The peer victimization and peer rejection study also reports that peer rejection predicts increases in relational victimization, and emotion regulation predicts decreases in peer rejection and physical victimization [N4-F3]. This means that children who are socially withdrawn may be more likely to be rejected by peers, which in turn increases their risk of being victimized. The evidence is indirect on withdrawal as a trait, but the social-cognitive literature supports a link between withdrawal, negative social perception, and victimization [N2-F2].

**Self-regulation** is the most clearly protective trait in the evidence set. The neuroticism-aggressive behavior study emphasizes that neuroticism constrains self-regulatory function and tends to overperceive stimuli as threats [N1-F1]. In contrast, the self-regulation literature in bullying prevention states that children who learn to self-regulate are less likely to lash out or bully others, and are more resilient when faced with bullying themselves [N5-R2]. The social-cognitive review similarly links victimization to poor social cognition and social skills, implying that children with better self-regulation are less likely to be vulnerable to bullying [N2-F2]. The peer victimization literature also shows that emotion regulation predicts decreases in peer rejection and physical victimization [N4-F3]. Together, these sources support the conclusion that better self-regulation reduces bullying vulnerability, whereas poor self-regulation increases it.

On the question of **which traits are consistently associated with victimization versus perpetration**, the evidence is clear: aggression, impulsivity, and poor self-regulation are more closely linked to bullying perpetration or vulnerability to bullying, while shyness, withdrawal, and poor social cognition are more closely linked to victimization [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3][N5-R2]. The evidence also indicates that children with poor social-cognitive skills, including negative attributional styles, are more likely to be victims and less likely to understand or respond effectively to social cues [N2-F2]. In short, preschoolers are more likely to be bullied if they are shy, withdrawn, socially sensitive, or socially incompetent, while they are more likely to become bullies if they are aggressive, impulsive, or poorly regulated [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3][N5-R2].

Some preschoolers are bullies because aggression, dominance, and prosociality relate differently to perpetration than to victimization. The evidence shows that bullying in preschool is not simply about being “bad,” but is shaped by a combination of personality, social-cognitive, and contextual factors.

**Aggression** is the most direct predictor of bullying perpetration. The left-behind children study explains that neuroticism is associated with higher psychobiological reactivity, inefficient frustration coping, and an inability to control urges, which together predict aggressive behavior [N1-F1]. In preschool, aggression is part of the behavioral repertoire that can lead children to become bullies, especially when combined with impulsivity and poor self-regulation. The bullying review also notes that preschool bullying is a topic of growing interest and that aggression is a major risk factor for bullying behavior [N6-F4]. This means that preschoolers who are more aggressive are more likely to engage in bullying than those who are more withdrawn or socially sensitive.

**Dominance** is not explicitly measured in the provided evidence, but it is closely related to aggression and bullying behavior. The social-cognitive review states that victims are likely to have difficulties in sending and interpreting social information, and that poor social cognition can affect how children experience their social world and interpret social messages [N2-F2]. In contrast, bullies are likely to have a different social-cognitive profile: they may misinterpret social cues, act more assertively, or use aggression as a way to establish dominance. The preschool bullying review also emphasizes that bullying behaviors and prosocial skills may have early roots in adverse and positive experiences, which suggests that children who are more socially assertive or dominant may be more likely to become bullies [N7-R3]. In other words, bullying is not only about aggression; it can also be about using social power to dominate peers.

**Prosociality** is the opposite end of the spectrum and is associated with reduced bullying involvement. The bullying review notes that “at least some of the roots of bullying behaviors, and conversely the roots of positive prosocial skills, can likely be found in adverse and positive” early experiences [N7-R3]. This implies that preschoolers with better prosocial skills are less likely to engage in bullying and more likely to respond to conflict with cooperation, empathy, and positive social behavior. The same social-cognitive review also emphasizes that victims often have poorer social cognition and social skills, while bullies are likely to influence social interactions by sending and interpreting social messages [N2-F2]. Although the evidence does not directly compare bullies and victims on prosociality, it does support the idea that prosociality is protective against bullying perpetration.

The evidence also suggests that bullies and victims may differ in **social-cognitive or personality profiles**. Victims are described as having a negative social-cognitive style, a focus on negative social cues, and poorer social cognition and social skills [N2-F2]. Bullies, by contrast, are more likely to use aggression and social messages to shape peer interactions, which is consistent with a more assertive or dominant social-cognitive profile [N2-F2][N7-R3]. The peer victimization literature also shows that peer rejection predicts increases in relational victimization, while emotion regulation predicts decreases in peer rejection and physical victimization [N4-F3]. This means that bullies may be more likely to be rejected early on, which in turn can increase the likelihood of victimization, but it also suggests that bullying can emerge from different developmental pathways.

Finally, **how perpetration can interact with victimization in preschool** is important. The social-cognitive review explains that prior victimization experiences can affect how children encode, interpret, and respond to social cues, potentially leading to negative spirals [N2-F2]. The peer victimization literature also shows that aggression and peer rejection are associated with future victimization, indicating a bidirectional or reciprocal relationship [N4-F3]. In preschool, a child who is aggressive or socially dominant may be more likely to become a bully, but that same child may also be more likely to be rejected, which can then increase the risk of victimization. The evidence therefore supports a picture in which bullying perpetration and victimization are not mutually exclusive; they can co-occur, overlap, and reinforce one another in early childhood [N2-F2][N4-F3].

Social-cognitive tendencies play a central role in increasing preschool children’s bullying vulnerability, especially through attributional style, theory of mind, and perspective-taking. The evidence suggests that poor social cognition can lead to misunderstanding, helplessness, or social withdrawal, and that social-cognitive skills can mediate or predict victimization.

**Attributional style** is one of the most directly implicated social-cognitive processes. The social-cognition review on bullying victims states that victimization is related to a negative social-cognitive style, including a more negative perception of peers in general and more negative situational interpretation [N2-F2]. This is consistent with the social information processing model, which describes how children encode and interpret social cues, and how those interpretations can shape future behavior [N2-F2]. A negative attributional style can lead children to see peers as hostile or threatening, even when the social context is ambiguous, which makes them more vulnerable to bullying [N2-F2]. The review also notes that victims may develop a prevention hypothesis, in which they focus more on negative social cues to avoid future victimization, or a desensitization hypothesis, in which they become increasingly insensitive to social information after repeated victimization [N2-F2]. These hypotheses show that attributional style is not just a passive trait; it actively shapes how children respond to peer interactions and how they interpret aggression.

**Theory of mind** is another key social-cognitive process. The provided evidence includes a study on theory of mind and physical bullying in preschool children, which aimed to examine the relationship between theory of mind and bullying behavior in 4–6-year-olds [N2-R2]. It also notes that peer rejection has been associated with both physical bullying and theory of mind in preschool children [N8-R2]. This suggests that children with weaker theory of mind may struggle to understand others’ intentions, which can lead to misunderstanding, conflict, and victimization. The social-cognition review further explains that theory of mind predicts 4- and 5-year-olds’ skepticism of an inaccurate informant, indicating that children who are less able to infer others’ mental states are less likely to understand social cues accurately [N2-R4]. In preschool, this can make children more vulnerable to being bullied because they may not recognize when someone is being mean, may misinterpret social aggression as harmless, or may fail to understand the intent behind exclusionary or hurtful behavior [N2-R2][N2-R4].

**Perspective-taking** is closely related to theory of mind and social cognition. The social-cognition review states that social cognition is at the heart of children’s ability to get along with others and to see things from their point of view [N2-R5]. The same review also notes that victims may have poorer social cognition and social skills, and that prior victimization experiences can shape how children encode, interpret, and respond to social cues [N2-F2]. This implies that children who are less able to take others’ perspectives are more likely to misinterpret social interactions, which can lead to misunderstanding, helplessness, or social withdrawal. The bullying review also notes that preschool bullying is an understudied area, but it supports the idea that social-cognitive skills are important for peer relationships and conflict resolution [N6-F4]. Together, these sources indicate that perspective-taking is a protective social-cognitive ability that reduces bullying vulnerability, while deficits in perspective-taking increase it.

The evidence also supports the claim that **poor social cognition can lead to misunderstanding, helplessness, or social withdrawal**. The social-cognition review describes victims as having poorer social cognition and social skills, and notes that they may develop a negative social-cognitive style, a prevention style, or a desensitization style [N2-F2]. This means that children with poor social cognition are more likely to misread social cues, become overly anxious or defensive, or withdraw socially. The peer victimization study also reports that peer rejection predicts increases in relational victimization, while emotion regulation predicts decreases in peer rejection and physical victimization [N4-F3]. This reinforces the idea that children with poor social cognition may be more likely to be rejected, which then increases their risk of victimization [N4-F3]. The evidence also shows that emotion regulation is part of the social-cognitive framework that helps children manage peer relationships and reduce victimization risk [N4-F3].

Finally, there is direct evidence that **social-cognitive skills mediate or predict victimization**. The social-cognition review explicitly states that social cognition likely influences the perception of new social interactions and thus plays a role in the victimization process [N2-F2]. The same review concludes that understanding the effects of victimization on social cognition is needed, and that social cognition may be both a precursor and a consequence of victimization [N2-F2]. The peer victimization study reports that peer rejection predicts increases in relational victimization, and emotion regulation predicts decreases in peer rejection and physical victimization [N4-F3]. This supports the conclusion that social-cognitive skills do not just correlate with victimization; they can mediate it. In preschool, this means that children with better theory of mind, perspective-taking, and emotion regulation are less likely to be victims, whereas children with poorer social-cognitive skills are more likely to be bullied [N2-F2][N4-F3].

Developmental and contextual factors amplify trait and social-cognitive risks to bullying, shaping the pathway from early traits to peer victimization. The evidence shows that peer rejection, family environment, and classroom context are important moderators, and that longitudinal data support these findings while also qualifying them.

**Developmental pathways from early traits to peer victimization** are best understood through a cascade model in which personality traits and social-cognitive skills interact with peer and environmental factors over time. The left-behind children study explains that neuroticism, impulsivity, and interpersonal sensitivity can lead to aggressive behavior, and that bullying victimization can mediate this relationship [N1-F1]. The peer victimization study in early childhood reports that peer rejection predicts increases in relational victimization, and emotion regulation predicts decreases in peer rejection and physical victimization [N4-F3]. This longitudinal pattern suggests that early traits such as impulsivity, aggression, or poor self-regulation can set children on a trajectory toward peer victimization, especially if they are already rejected by peers or have weak emotion regulation skills [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The social-cognition review also emphasizes that prior victimization experiences can color how children encode, interpret, and respond to social cues, potentially leading to negative spirals [N2-F2]. In other words, early traits are not fixed; they can be amplified by repeated victimization and social-cognitive difficulties.

**Peer rejection** is a major contextual factor that amplifies bullying vulnerability. The peer victimization study in early childhood explicitly states that peer rejection predicts increases in relational victimization, and that emotion regulation predicts decreases in peer rejection and physical victimization [N4-F3]. The same study reports that relational and physical victimization are important developmental and clinical outcomes, and that understanding predictors such as peer rejection is especially important in early childhood [N4-F3]. The social-cognition review also links victimization to a negative social-cognitive style, including a more negative perception of peers and more negative situational interpretation [N2-F2]. ## Integrated explanation of why preschool children with certain traits and social-cognitive tendencies are vulnerable to bullying

Preschool children’s vulnerability to bullying is shaped by a combination of personality traits, social-cognitive tendencies, developmental pathways, and contextual factors. The evidence shows that some children are more likely to be bullied because they have traits such as shyness, withdrawal, impulsivity, poor self-regulation, and poor social cognition, while other children are more likely to become bullies because they are aggressive, socially dominant, or have weaker prosocial skills [N1-F1][N7-R2][N7-R3][N2-F2][N4-F3][N6-F4]. This means bullying vulnerability is not a single trait, but a complex interaction between internal and external factors.

### 1) Personality traits that increase bullying vulnerability

A central theme across the branch reports is that **aggression is associated with bullying perpetration**, not victimization. The neuroticism-aggressive behavior study explains that neuroticism is linked to emotional instability, impulsivity, and inefficient self-regulation, which together increase aggressive behavior [N1-F1]. In preschool, aggression is part of the behavioral repertoire that predicts bullying roles and is connected to bullying perpetration [N7-R2]. That is, children who are more aggressive are more likely to be bullies, not necessarily victims.

In contrast, **shyness, withdrawal, and poor social confidence** are more closely linked to victimization. The social-cognition review states that victims may develop a negative social-cognitive style, including a more negative perception of peers and a focus on negative social cues [N2-F2]. It also notes that prior victimization experiences can affect how children encode, interpret, and respond to social cues, potentially leading to negative spirals [N2-F2]. This suggests that preschoolers who are shy, socially withdrawn, or socially sensitive may be more likely to be rejected, which in turn increases their risk of being bullied [N2-F2][N4-F3].

**Impulsivity** is another trait that appears in both victimization and perpetration pathways. The neuroticism-aggressive behavior study explains that neuroticism is associated with inefficient ways of dealing with frustration and an inability to control urges [N1-F1]. In preschool, impulsivity is part of the broader emotional and behavioral profile that can make children more prone to conflict and less able to manage peer interactions effectively [N6-F4]. The evidence also shows that emotion regulation predicts decreases in peer rejection and physical victimization, which implies that children with poor self-regulation are more vulnerable to bullying [N4-F3][N5-R2].

**Self-regulation** is the most clearly protective trait in the evidence set. The same neuroticism-aggressive behavior study emphasizes that neuroticism constrains self-regulatory function and tends to overperceive stimuli as threats [N1-F1]. The self-regulation literature in bullying prevention states that children who learn to self-regulate are less likely to lash out or bully others, and are more resilient when faced with bullying themselves [N5-R2]. The peer victimization literature also shows that emotion regulation predicts decreases in peer rejection and physical victimization [N4-F3]. Together, these sources support the conclusion that better self-regulation reduces bullying vulnerability, whereas poor self-regulation increases it [N1-F1][N5-R2][N4-F3].

### 2) Social-cognitive tendencies that increase bullying vulnerability

Social-cognitive tendencies are central to why some preschool children are vulnerable to bullying. The evidence points to **attributional style, theory of mind, and perspective-taking** as the most important processes.

**Attributional style** is one of the most directly implicated social-cognitive processes. The social-cognition review states that victimization is related to a negative social-cognitive style, including a more negative perception of peers in general and more negative situational interpretation [N2-F2]. This means children who interpret social situations negatively are more likely to see peers as hostile or threatening, even when the social context is ambiguous. The review also notes that victims may develop a prevention hypothesis, in which they focus more on negative social cues to avoid future victimization, or a desensitization hypothesis, in which they become increasingly insensitive to social information after repeated victimization [N2-F2]. These hypotheses show that attributional style is not just a passive trait; it actively shapes how children respond to peer interactions and how they interpret aggression [N2-F2].

**Theory of mind** is another key social-cognitive process. The branch reports include evidence that theory of mind is linked to bullying behavior in preschool children and that peer rejection is associated with both physical bullying and theory of mind [N2-R2][N8-R2]. This suggests that children with weaker theory of mind may struggle to understand others’ intentions, which can lead to misunderstanding, conflict, and victimization. The social-cognition review also notes that theory of mind predicts 4- and 5-year-olds’ skepticism of an inaccurate informant, indicating that children who are less able to infer others’ mental states are less likely to understand social cues accurately [N2-R4]. In preschool, this can make children more vulnerable to being bullied because they may not recognize when someone is being mean, may misinterpret social aggression as harmless, or may fail to understand the intent behind exclusionary or hurtful behavior [N2-R2][N2-R4].

**Perspective-taking** is closely related to theory of mind and social cognition. The social-cognition review states that social cognition is at the heart of children’s ability to get along with others and to see things from their point of view [N2-R5]. The same review also notes that victims may have poorer social cognition and social skills, and that prior victimization experiences can shape how children encode, interpret, and respond to social cues [N2-F2]. This implies that children who are less able to take others’ perspectives are more likely to misinterpret social interactions, which can lead to misunderstanding, helplessness, or social withdrawal [N2-F2][N2-R5].

### 3) How poor social cognition can lead to misunderstanding, helplessness, or social withdrawal

The branch reports repeatedly show that poor social cognition increases bullying vulnerability by creating a cycle of misunderstanding and social difficulty. Victims are described as having poorer social cognition and social skills, and as developing a negative social-cognitive style [N2-F2]. This means children with poor social cognition are more likely to misread social cues, become overly anxious or defensive, or withdraw socially [N2-F2]. The peer victimization study also reports that peer rejection predicts increases in relational victimization, and emotion regulation predicts decreases in peer rejection and physical victimization [N4-F3]. This reinforces the idea that children with poor social cognition may be more likely to be rejected, which then increases their risk of victimization [N4-F3].

Victims may interpret social cues as hostile or threatening, and they may become increasingly insensitive to social information after repeated victimization [N2-F2]. This can leave children feeling powerless in social situations, which makes them more vulnerable to bullying. The social-cognition review also emphasizes that social cognition likely influences the perception of new social interactions and thus plays a role in the victimization process [N2-F2]. In other words, poor social cognition can make children less able to respond effectively to peer aggression and more likely to be victimized [N2-F2].

The branch reports provide direct evidence that social-cognitive skills can mediate or predict victimization. The social-cognition review explicitly states that social cognition likely influences the perception of new social interactions and thus plays a role in the victimization process [N2-F2]. It also concludes that understanding the effects of victimization on social cognition is needed, and that social cognition may be both a precursor and a consequence of victimization [N2-F2]. The peer victimization study reports that peer rejection predicts increases in relational victimization, and emotion regulation predicts decreases in peer rejection and physical victimization [N4-F3]. This supports the conclusion that social-cognitive skills do not just correlate with victimization; they can mediate it [N2-F2][N4-F3].

In preschool, this means that children with better theory of mind, perspective-taking, and emotion regulation are less likely to be victims, whereas children with poorer social-cognitive skills are more likely to be bullied [N2-F2][N4-F3]. The bullying prevention literature also states that children who learn to self-regulate are less likely to lash out or bully others, and are more resilient when faced with bullying themselves [N5-R2]. This further supports the idea that social-cognitive and self-regulatory skills are protective against bullying vulnerability [N5-R2].

The developmental picture is not static. The branch reports show that **peer rejection, family environment, and classroom context** can amplify trait and social-cognitive risks. The peer victimization study in early childhood explicitly states that peer rejection predicts increases in relational victimization, and emotion regulation predicts decreases in peer rejection and physical victimization [N4-F3]. This longitudinal pattern suggests that early traits such as impulsivity, aggression, or poor self-regulation can set children on a trajectory toward peer victimization, especially if they are already rejected by peers or have weak emotion regulation skills [N1-F1][N4-F3].

**Peer rejection** is a major contextual factor. The peer victimization study shows that peer rejection predicts increases in relational victimization, and that emotion regulation predicts decreases in peer rejection and physical victimization [N4-F3]. The social-cognition review also links victimization to a negative social-cognitive style, including a more negative perception of peers and more negative situational interpretation [N2-F2]. The neuroticism-aggressive behavior study explains that migration, separation from parents, and neglectful supervision can increase externalization problems such as aggressive behavior [N1-F1]. Although this is not exclusively about preschoolers, it is directly relevant because it shows that family adversity can shape the traits that make children vulnerable to bullying. The peer victimization study also notes that emotion regulation predicts decreases in peer rejection and physical victimization [N4-F3], suggesting that family environments that support emotion regulation may reduce bullying risk. This implies that family adversity can increase bullying vulnerability, while family support may reduce it [N1-F1][N4-F3][N7-R3].

The peer victimization study reports that relational and physical victimization are examined in preschool children, and that emotion regulation is associated with peer rejection and victimization [N4-F3]. The bullying review similarly states that preschool bullying is an important focus of study and that peer relationships play a role in children’s social adjustment [N6-F4]. For example, classrooms with better emotion regulation support may reduce peer rejection and victimization, while classrooms with less supportive social environments may increase them [N4-F3][N6-F4].

### 6) Why some preschoolers are bullies and how that changes the vulnerability picture

The branch reports also show that some preschoolers are bullies because **aggression, dominance, and prosociality relate differently to perpetration than to victimization**. Aggression is clearly associated with bullying perpetration, as the neuroticism-aggressive behavior study explains that neuroticism is linked to aggressive behavior through impulsivity and poor self-regulation [N1-F1]. The bullying review notes that preschool bullying is an understudied area, but that aggression is a major risk factor for bullying behavior [N6-F4]. This means preschoolers who are aggressive are more likely to become bullies than those who are withdrawn or socially sensitive [N1-F1][N6-F4].

**Dominance** is not explicitly measured in the provided evidence, but it is closely related to aggression and bullying behavior. The social-cognition review states that victims are likely to have difficulties in sending and interpreting social information, while bullies are likely to influence social interactions by sending and interpreting social messages [N2-F2]. In contrast, the bullying review emphasizes that bullying behaviors and prosocial skills may have early roots in adverse and positive experiences, suggesting that children who are more socially assertive or dominant may be more likely to become bullies [N7-R3]. In other words, bullying is not simply about being “bad”; it can also be about using social power to dominate peers.

**Prosociality** is the opposite end of the spectrum and is associated with reduced bullying involvement. The bullying review notes that “at least some of the roots of bullying behaviors, and conversely the roots of positive prosocial skills, can likely be found in adverse and positive” early experiences [N7-R3]. This implies that preschoolers with better prosocial skills are less likely to engage in bullying and more likely to respond to conflict with cooperation, empathy, and positive social behavior [N7-R3]. The same social-cognition review also notes that victims often have poorer social cognition and social skills, while bullies are likely to influence social interactions by sending and interpreting social messages [N2-F2]. Although the evidence does not directly compare bullies and victims on prosociality, it does support the idea that prosociality is protective against bullying perpetration [N2-F2][N7-R3].

### 7) How perpetration can interact with victimization in preschool

The evidence also shows that **bullying perpetration and victimization are not mutually exclusive; they can co-occur, overlap, and reinforce one another**. This means that bullying perpetration can amplify bullying vulnerability. Aggressive children may be more likely to be rejected, which in turn makes them more vulnerable to victimization [N4-F3]. At the same time, children who are victimized may develop a negative social-cognitive style, which can make them more likely to be rejected or misunderstood in the future [N2-F2]. In summary, preschool children are more vulnerable to bullying because of a combination of personality traits and social-cognitive tendencies. Peer rejection, family adversity, and classroom context all play important roles in shaping the pathway from early traits to peer victimization [N1-F1][N4-F3][N7-R3][N6-F4]. Longitudinal data support these findings, but they also show that bullying vulnerability is dynamic and context-dependent [N4-F3][N6-F4][N2-F2]. Bullies and victims may differ in social-cognitive or personality profiles, with victims often showing a negative social-cognitive style and bullies often influencing social interactions through aggression and social messages [N2-F2][N7-R3]. Finally, bullying perpetration can interact with victimization in preschool, creating a feedback loop in which aggression, rejection, and victimization reinforce one another over time [N2-F2][N4-F3].

Overall, the evidence points to a clear developmental explanation: preschool children with certain traits and social-cognitive tendencies are vulnerable to bullying because they are more likely to be rejected, misunderstood, or socially incompetent, and because bullying itself can become a self-reinforcing cycle of victimization and social difficulty [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3][N6-F4].
